paragraphs: Large learning rates can produce training behavior that classical gradient descent analyses struggle to explain. This paper studies two related phenomena: progressive sharpening and the edge of stability. Rather than analyzing a large network directly, it constructs a two-layer network with a two-dimensional input. One input dimension matters for predicting the response, while the other is irrelevant.

Within this small model, the authors rigorously establish progressive sharpening and self-stabilization under large learning rates. Their analysis tracks both training dynamics and sharpness throughout the gradient descent trajectory. Because the results are non-asymptotic, they address behavior during training rather than describing only what happens in a limiting regime.

The paper also connects this example to broader theoretical approaches by reconciling their accounts of a well-behaved stable set and extending an existing gradient-flow sharpness analysis. The contribution is an analytically tractable setting that connects parameter behavior with input structure. Its findings could inform optimization strategies, although that practical implication is presented as a possibility.
neurips-2025-a-minimalist-example-of-edg.tldr: A small two-layer network enables rigorous analysis of progressive sharpening and self-stabilization during gradient descent with large learning rates.

paragraphs: Invisible watermarks aim to identify AI-generated images without visibly changing them. Their usefulness depends on surviving attempts to remove them while retaining image quality. This report describes Erasing the Invisible, a competition and benchmark created to test that resilience through a shared evaluation process.

The competition used Black-box and Beige-box tracks to represent different levels of attacker knowledge about the watermarks. It received 2,722 submissions from 298 teams. Participants obtained real-time evaluation feedback, while the final rankings included human verification. This structure supported a large collection of attacks assessed within a common framework.

On average, the top five teams in each track removed watermarks from at least 89% of images while preserving high visual quality. These results expose substantial vulnerabilities in the watermarking methods tested. The report also releases the dataset, evaluation tools, and competition results, giving future work a concrete basis for comparing attacks and developing stronger defenses. The central contribution is both evidence of weaknesses and infrastructure for measuring progress.
neurips-2025-a-technical-report-on-erasi.tldr: A large watermark stress-testing competition found that leading attacks could remove watermarks from at least 89% of images on average while preserving high visual quality.

paragraphs: Language models can evaluate many responses quickly, but their ratings can differ systematically from human assessments. Bridge addresses this mismatch with a statistical framework that supports both assigning an absolute score and choosing between two responses. Its aim is to refine automated evaluations while making their disagreements with people easier to understand.

The framework assumes an underlying human preference score for each prompt-response pair. It then models the language model's deviations using linear transformations of covariates: variables intended to capture sources of disagreement. This separates the preference being estimated from structured patterns in how an automated judge departs from it. The authors also provide an efficient fitting algorithm with asymptotic guarantees for statistical inference.

The evaluation uses six language-model judges and two benchmarks, BigGen Bench and Chatbot Arena. Bridge improves agreement with human ratings according to accuracy, calibration, and KL divergence, while revealing systematic gaps between the two kinds of judges. The findings support statistical adjustment as a useful way to improve automated evaluation and investigate its recurring discrepancies.
neurips-2025-bridging-human-and-llm-judg.tldr: Bridge models systematic differences between human and language-model judgments to improve rating agreement and reveal recurring sources of disagreement.

paragraphs: Role-playing models commonly receive a written character description and must work out how it applies to each situation. This paper converts those descriptions into executable character profiles. An LLM produces functions that examine a scene and return assertions grounded in the character's behavioral logic, making that logic an explicit part of response preparation.

The functions combine ordinary conditional branches with semantic questions that the role-playing model answers as true, false, or unknown. They also support randomness within the behavioral rules. This makes character behavior easier to inspect and revise, while providing a direct mechanism for consistent rule execution and controlled variation across responses.

The authors evaluate the approach using 83 characters and 5,141 scenes curated from Fandom, with natural language inference scoring against reference expectations. They report improvements in persistence, updatability, and behavioral diversity. Moving substantial reasoning into preprocessing also allows models with one billion parameters to deliver high-quality role-playing in their experiments, supporting the approach as a lightweight foundation for local agents.
neurips-2025-codifying-character-logic-i.tldr: Executable character profiles make role-playing behavior more consistent, editable, and controllably varied, with reported benefits even for one-billion-parameter models.

paragraphs: A person's actions reflect both what they want to accomplish and how their attention is distributed. This paper formalizes attention-aware inverse planning: inferring attentional biases from observed behavior. The motivation is that systems interacting with people should account for systematic differences in what people attend to, including during everyday activities such as driving.

The authors explain how this inference problem differs from standard inverse reinforcement learning. The target is an attentional strategy that influences behavior, so the account must explicitly represent that source of variation. Their proposed approach combines deep reinforcement learning with computational cognitive modeling, connecting action selection to a structured description of attention.

The demonstration infers the attentional strategies of reinforcement-learning agents in real-life driving scenarios selected from the Waymo Open Dataset. These experiments support the scalability of the proposed inference approach in that setting. The distinction matters: the reported demonstration concerns agents in driving scenarios, while the broader motivation is understanding cognitive biases in people. The paper provides a formal problem definition and an approach for studying that connection.
neurips-2025-estimating-cognitive-biases.tldr: Attention-aware inverse planning estimates attentional biases from actions, with a demonstration recovering reinforcement-learning agents' strategies in driving scenarios.

paragraphs: Semantic matching identifies corresponding regions across images. Features from pretrained image models can support this task without additional training, but simply joining features together can leave useful information poorly combined. Fuse2Match investigates how to combine Stable Diffusion 3, Stable Diffusion, and DINO more effectively for this purpose.

The authors find that Stable Diffusion 3 distributes semantic information across several transformer layers and timesteps. They therefore fuse information at multiple levels to obtain more discriminative features. They also identify inconsistent feature distributions across models as a problem for naive fusion. Their solution weights each model's contribution using confidence scores derived from uncertainty in its matches.

These weights adapt at individual pixels, allowing the combined representation to draw differently on the models across an image. The fusion requires no training. Experiments on SPair-71k, PF-Pascal, and PSC6K show significant improvements over strong baselines. The results support both gathering dispersed information within Stable Diffusion 3 and using matching confidence to combine heterogeneous pretrained features.
neurips-2025-fuse2match-training-free-fu.tldr: Fuse2Match improves zero-shot semantic matching by combining pretrained image-model features with pixel-specific weights based on matching confidence.

paragraphs: GUI agents must connect an instruction with the appropriate region of a screen. Generating coordinates as text can poorly align meaning with location, penalize multiple valid click targets, and mismatch the patch-based visual features used by the model. GUI-Actor addresses these issues by predicting action regions through attention.

Its action head aligns a dedicated action token with relevant visual patch tokens, producing one or more candidate regions in a single forward pass. A separate grounding verifier evaluates those candidates and selects a plausible region for execution. This representation accommodates regions containing valid alternatives instead of requiring a single textual coordinate prediction.

GUI-Actor improves results across multiple grounding benchmarks and generalizes better to unseen resolutions and layouts. On ScreenSpot-Pro, its seven-billion-parameter versions score 40.7 and 44.6 with two different backbones, compared with 38.1 for UI-TARS-72B, using fewer parameters and training data. With the verifier, training only the approximately 100-million-parameter action head while freezing the backbone also reaches performance comparable to previous leading models.
neurips-2025-gui-actor-coordinate-free-v.tldr: GUI-Actor uses attention over screen patches and a verifier to locate action regions, improving GUI grounding with relatively small trainable components.

paragraphs: Interactive language-model applications need quick responses, while offline jobs such as data synthesis prioritize processing volume. Assigning separate machines to these workloads makes their service requirements easier to manage but can leave resources underused. HyGen is a serving system designed to run both workloads together while preserving their service-level objectives.

The system explicitly accounts for interference between requests. A latency predictor estimates how long a batch will execute, and an SLO-aware profiler measures the latency effects of sharing resources. These mechanisms inform offline scheduling policies that seek higher throughput while respecting service requirements and preventing offline requests from being indefinitely postponed.

Evaluations on production workloads report throughput gains of up to 3.9–5.8 times over online and hybrid serving baselines while meeting latency objectives. The result shows that coordinating workloads with different priorities can substantially improve utilization in the tested settings. HyGen's contribution is the combination of performance estimation and scheduling policies that make shared serving responsive to interference.
neurips-2025-hygen-efficient-llm-serving.tldr: HyGen co-locates interactive and offline LLM requests using interference-aware scheduling, reporting substantial throughput gains while maintaining latency objectives.

paragraphs: Patent-product image retrieval searches for patent images that resemble a product photograph, helping identify potential infringements. The task faces two difficulties: products can belong to object categories poorly represented in pretraining, and colorful photographs differ strongly from binary patent drawings. The paper treats this as an open-set retrieval problem and introduces a dataset for studying it.

The dataset includes 439 test product-patent pairs, a search pool of 727,921 patents, and 3,799,695 unlabeled pretraining images. The proposed IDAMA method uses edge detection to map both photographs and patent drawings into an intermediate sketch domain. This reduces the visual discrepancy between the two image types before comparing their representations.

IDAMA also includes a Morphology Analogy Filter that selects discriminative patent images through visual-feature-based analogical reasoning. Experiments on the new dataset report a 7.58 mAR improvement over baseline methods. Together, the dataset and method provide evidence that shared visual representation and shape-oriented selection can improve retrieval across the product-to-patent domain gap.
neurips-2025-intermediate-domain-alignme.tldr: IDAMA improves product-to-patent image retrieval by mapping images into a shared sketch domain and selecting informative patent images through morphology analogy.

paragraphs: Learning curves describe how a model's performance changes as its training set grows. They help researchers study scaling and make faster choices among models or hyperparameters. These uses often assume curves are monotone and convex: performance improves with more data and follows a regular shape. LCDB 1.1 examines how often those assumptions hold.

The authors build a large database of densely measured learning curves, including modern learners such as CatBoost, TabNet, RealMLP, and TabPFN. Statistical analysis finds significant departures from the expected behavior in approximately 15% of curves, nearly twice the frequency of earlier estimates. The tendency varies across learners, and changing feature scaling rarely resolves it.

The paper also evaluates how these irregularities affect curve fitting and model selection, finding substantial challenges for both. This matters because methods that rely on a regular curve can encounter behavior their assumptions do not capture. LCDB 1.1 supplies a benchmark for studying those cases and improving methods that make decisions from learning curves.
neurips-2025-lcdb-1-1-a-database-illustr.tldr: LCDB 1.1 finds statistically significant irregular behavior in approximately 15% of learning curves, challenging assumptions used in curve fitting and model selection.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves an outer objective whose value depends on the solution to an inner optimization problem. This structure appears in many machine-learning settings, but its learning theory has largely focused on parametric formulations. The paper studies a nonparametric version in which the inner problem searches over a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

That kernel-based function space supports rich approximation while giving the authors a mathematical structure for analysis. Using empirical process theory, they derive finite-sample generalization bounds for Kernel Bilevel Optimization. These bounds address how conclusions based on a finite dataset relate to the underlying learning problem, rather than treating the available sample as the entire target.

The authors then use the bounds to assess the statistical accuracy of gradient-based methods applied to an empirical discretization of the problem. A synthetic instrumental-variable regression task provides a numerical illustration of the theoretical findings. The main contribution is a learning-theoretic foundation for this kernel setting, connecting function-space optimization, finite data, and the accuracy of practical gradient-based procedures.
neurips-2025-learning-theory-for-kernel-.tldr: The paper develops finite-sample generalization bounds for kernel bilevel optimization and uses them to analyze the statistical accuracy of gradient-based methods.

paragraphs: Editing a generative model is easier when the relevant knowledge can be connected to particular parts of the network. This paper studies that question in diffusion transformers, where knowledge localization has received less attention than in UNet-based models. It proposes a method designed to locate knowledge across transformer blocks without being specific to one model or knowledge category.

The authors evaluate the method on PixArt-α, FLUX, and SANA across six knowledge categories. They report that the identified blocks have interpretable roles and are causally connected to how knowledge appears in generated outputs. This causal connection supports using the localized blocks as targets for changes to the model's behavior.

The paper applies localized fine-tuning to personalization and knowledge unlearning. In both applications, targeted updates reduce computation, improve task-specific performance, and better preserve general model behavior, with little interference to unrelated or surrounding content. The findings connect an interpretability question about where knowledge resides with a practical strategy for making more focused model edits.
neurips-2025-localizing-knowledge-in-dif.tldr: Localizing knowledge within diffusion-transformer blocks enables targeted fine-tuning that improves personalization and unlearning while reducing interference with other behavior.

paragraphs: Image generators commonly work with fixed resolutions and square formats. This paper introduces native-resolution synthesis, which treats variation in image size and aspect ratio as part of generative modeling itself. The central technical challenge is handling visual-token sequences whose lengths change with the image format.

The proposed Native-resolution diffusion Transformer, or NiT, explicitly models resolution and aspect ratio during denoising. It learns from images spanning different formats within one architecture. A single NiT model achieves state-of-the-art performance on both the 256-by-256 and 512-by-512 ImageNet benchmarks, supporting the value of learning across resolutions in a shared model.

The authors also report zero-shot generation at resolutions and aspect ratios not seen during training, using a model pretrained solely on ImageNet. Examples include 1024-by-1024 and 1536-by-1536 images, as well as 16:9, 3:1, and 4:3 formats. These results demonstrate strong generalization in the evaluated settings and suggest that variable-length visual modeling could connect image generation more closely with methods used in advanced language models.
neurips-2025-native-resolution-image-syn.tldr: NiT models varying image resolutions and aspect ratios directly, achieving strong ImageNet results and zero-shot generation at previously unseen formats.

paragraphs: Dynamic scenes are difficult to represent in a way that supports both complex interactions and straightforward editing. Two-layer neural atlases make appearance editable in two dimensions but struggle when several objects overlap and interact. Scene graphs capture richer spatial relationships, yet their volumetric representations can be difficult to edit consistently across views.

Neural Atlas Graphs combine these ideas by assigning a view-dependent neural atlas to every graph node. The resulting representation supports two-dimensional appearance changes alongside three-dimensional ordering and positioning of scene elements. It is fitted at test time and enables high-resolution edits such as replacing driving-scene backgrounds or changing vehicle appearance.

On the Waymo Open Dataset, the authors report state-of-the-art quantitative results, including a five-decibel PSNR improvement over existing methods. They also evaluate human- and animal-centered videos in DAVIS, reporting more than a seven-decibel advantage over recent matting and video-editing baselines. These findings show that the hybrid representation supports both editable driving scenes and a broader collection of dynamic video content.
neurips-2025-neural-atlas-graphs-for-dyn.tldr: Neural Atlas Graphs combine editable image-based nodes with three-dimensional scene organization, improving reconstruction quality and enabling complex dynamic-scene edits.

paragraphs: Local convergence studies how the neighborhoods of sparse random graphs behave as the graphs grow. This paper introduces color convergence, a new formulation based on the Weisfeiler–Leman algorithm. Its central result connects a graph-theoretic notion of limiting behavior with the behavior of message-passing graph neural networks.

Specifically, color convergence fully characterizes the random graphs that are well-behaved in the limit for these neural networks. This provides a criterion tied to the kind of local information processing that message-passing models perform. The authors also introduce the Refined Configuration Model, extending the existing configuration model into a broader random-graph construction.

The new model is universal with respect to local convergence within the class of locally tree-like random graph models. That class includes Erdős–Rényi, stochastic block, and configuration models. The framework further completely characterizes the random trees arising as local limits of such graphs. Its universality is therefore a precise statement about this local-convergence setting, linking a broad family of graph models through their limiting neighborhood structure.
neurips-2025-on-local-limits-of-sparse-r.tldr: Color convergence characterizes well-behaved graph limits for message-passing networks, while the Refined Configuration Model unifies locally tree-like random graphs under local convergence.

paragraphs: Diffusion generators can produce high-quality samples, but repeatedly applying their sampling procedure is computationally expensive. The Koopman Distillation Model addresses this cost through offline distillation into a single generation step. It builds on the observation that diffusion trajectories have semantic structure and can be studied as dynamical systems.

Koopman theory represents nonlinear dynamics through linear evolution in a transformed space. KDM encodes a noisy input into such a space, advances it with a learned linear operator, and decodes the result into a clean sample. The paper provides theoretical support: under mild assumptions, the learned diffusion dynamics admit a finite-dimensional Koopman representation. It also connects closeness in the transformed space with semantic similarity in generated outputs.

That semantic connection supports aligning trajectories during distillation while retaining meaningful output structure. On standard offline-distillation benchmarks, KDM achieves state-of-the-art performance, with FID improvements of up to 40% using one generation step. The result combines a conditional theoretical account of diffusion dynamics with empirical evidence for efficient single-step generation.
neurips-2025-one-step-offline-distillati.tldr: KDM distills diffusion generation into one step by learning linear dynamics in a transformed space, with reported FID improvements of up to 40%.

paragraphs: Point-cloud synthesis generates new collections of points from an input distribution. The paper tackles this task through the representation of the data: it develops an encoding that uses inner products to capture geometric and topological characteristics. The aim is to provide an efficient description of point clouds that can be integrated into deep-learning models.

The representation comes with provable expressivity properties, giving mathematical support for its ability to represent the relevant structure. This is a distinct contribution alongside its practical efficiency. The paper places the encoding inside learning models and studies it across reconstruction, generation, and interpolation, covering several ways a model can use or produce point-cloud data.

The authors report high quality on these tasks and inference times orders of magnitude faster than existing methods. These findings suggest that the choice of representation can be central to both output quality and computational cost in point-cloud synthesis. The contribution combines a theoretically supported encoding with empirical evidence that it can support several tasks efficiently.
neurips-2025-point-cloud-synthesis-using.tldr: An inner-product-based point-cloud encoding combines provable expressivity with high-quality reconstruction, generation, and interpolation at substantially faster inference speeds.

paragraphs: Sampling becomes difficult when a probability distribution has several separated regions of high probability, even in low dimensions. This paper presents a sampling algorithm for a broad distribution class that includes all Gaussian mixtures. Its central guarantee is polynomial query complexity in the parameters governing multimodality, with the dimension held fixed.

The algorithm simulates a diffusion process in reverse time. To obtain the intermediate score functions needed for this process, it uses a self-normalized Monte Carlo estimator. This gives the method a way to construct the intermediate guidance required by its sampling procedure without needing prior knowledge of where the distribution's modes are located.

The authors report that the method avoids metastability and relaxes the usual log-smoothness assumption, which had excluded general Gaussian mixtures from earlier results. They identify their polynomial query guarantee as the first for this broad setting. The fixed-dimension qualification is central to interpreting that result: the guarantee concerns how difficulty scales with multimodality parameters when dimension is not growing.
neurips-2025-sampling-from-multi-modal-d.tldr: A reverse-diffusion sampler achieves polynomial query complexity for a broad multimodal distribution class, including Gaussian mixtures, when dimension is fixed.

paragraphs: Language models trained on shorter contexts can struggle when given longer ones. This paper studies how an attention mechanism should behave as context length changes. The authors propose two properties they expect effective long-context attention to possess: scale invariance in total attention and in attention sparsity.

They then show that, under a Gaussian assumption, a simple position-dependent transformation of attention logits is sufficient to satisfy both properties. Logits are the scores from which attention weights are formed, so the intervention acts directly on how attention is allocated. The theoretical statement establishes sufficiency under the assumption; the proposed properties are motivated expectations about effective mechanisms.

Experiments find considerable validation-loss benefits when models trained on short contexts are evaluated zero-shot on longer contexts. The resulting attention scheme also performs effectively at long-context retrieval. Together, these findings support the proposed transformation as a way to improve length generalization, connecting desired scaling behavior with a concrete modification to attention and empirical tests on longer inputs.
neurips-2025-scale-invariant-attention-f.tldr: A position-dependent attention-logit transformation satisfies two proposed scaling properties under a Gaussian assumption and improves empirical generalization to longer contexts.

paragraphs: Instruction-based video editing needs examples that correctly carry out an edit while remaining consistent across frames. Existing datasets struggle with editing accuracy, temporal consistency, and diversity. Señorita-2M addresses this training-data problem by assembling a large collection of editing examples produced by specialized video-editing methods.

The authors organize editing into two broad classes and 18 subcategories. They create four new specialists and use or adapt 14 existing experts to generate examples for those subclasses. A filtering pipeline checks both visual content and instructions to improve data quality. The final dataset contains two million samples spanning different resolutions and frame counts.

To test its usefulness, the authors train multiple editing models using Wan2.1 and CogVideoX-5B as base video models. They report superior visual quality, strong consistency between frames, and effective instruction following. These results support combining task-specific expertise and filtering to build training data for broader editing capabilities. The contribution joins a structured account of editing tasks with a large dataset and training demonstrations across different base models.
neurips-2025-senorita-2m-a-high-quality-.tldr: Señorita-2M uses specialized editors and filtering to create two million instruction-based video-editing samples that support strong quality and frame consistency.

paragraphs: Dynamic algorithm configuration adjusts hyperparameters while an algorithm runs, reducing the need for manual trial and error. Multi-agent reinforcement learning can coordinate several different hyperparameters, but their decisions may depend on one another. For example, selecting an operator can determine which setting for that operator makes sense.

Seq-MADAC builds these dependencies into the configuration process. Its sequential advantage decomposition network uses action-order information when decomposing the advantage associated with decisions. This gives the learning framework an explicit way to account for the sequence in which related parameter choices are made, addressing a dependency that earlier approaches did not consider.

Experiments range from synthetic functions to configuring multi-objective optimization algorithms. The authors report better performance than state-of-the-art multi-agent reinforcement-learning methods and strong generalization across problem classes. These results support treating parameter dependencies as part of the configuration problem itself. The broader contribution is a framework for automated tuning that uses the structure among configuration choices during execution.
neurips-2025-sequential-multi-agent-dyna.tldr: Seq-MADAC improves dynamic algorithm configuration by using sequential multi-agent learning to account for dependencies among hyperparameter choices.

paragraphs: StableGuard brings watermark embedding and tamper detection into one framework for latent diffusion models. It integrates a binary watermark during image generation, addressing inconveniences and forensic reliability concerns associated with post-processing. The goal is to support both watermark verification for copyright protection and identification of image regions that have been altered.

The framework adds a lightweight residual adapter to a pretrained variational autoencoder. This Multiplexing Watermark VAE generates paired images with and without watermarks. Combining those pairs through random masks produces training examples for a forensic network, allowing the training data to be constructed within the framework.

The forensic network uses a mixture-of-experts design to combine overall watermark patterns, local signs of tampering, and frequency-domain information. It is optimized jointly with the watermarking component through self-supervised training, linking watermark embedding to forensic performance. Experiments report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods in image fidelity, watermark verification, and tamper localization. The contribution is an integrated generation-and-analysis system whose components are trained to support one another.
neurips-2025-stableguard-towards-unified.tldr: StableGuard jointly trains watermark embedding and forensic analysis within latent diffusion generation, improving image fidelity, watermark verification, and tamper localization.

paragraphs: Music arrangement can involve reinterpreting a piece, simplifying its instrumentation, or adding new parts. This paper develops a unified framework in which a single pretrained symbolic-music model handles these different scenarios. The aim is to support flexible transformations between instrumentations within one shared modeling approach.

The core training objective reconstructs segments while separating content and style at the token level. This organization enables any-to-any instrumentation transformations at inference time. The authors also introduce REMI-z, a structured tokenization scheme designed for multitrack symbolic music. It supports track-wise modeling and improves efficiency and effectiveness for both arrangement and unconditional generation.

The evaluation covers band arrangement, piano reduction, and drum arrangement, representing different kinds of transformation. The proposed method outperforms task-specific state-of-the-art systems in both objective measurements and perceptual evaluations. These findings support using a shared reconstruction objective and structured representation across arrangement tasks. They also suggest broader applicability to symbolic music-to-music transformations beyond the representative scenarios evaluated in the paper.
neurips-2025-unifying-symbolic-music-arr.tldr: A shared reconstruction objective and REMI-z tokenization let one symbolic-music model handle diverse arrangement tasks and outperform task-specific systems.

paragraphs: Heterogeneous graphs describe data containing different kinds of entities and relationships. Learning across them requires reconciling varied attributes and propagating information effectively. UniHG provides a joint multi-domain dataset for studying these problems, containing 77.31 million nodes, 564 million directed edges, and thousands of labels and attributes.

The paper combines the dataset with two learning strategies. First, semantic alignment places descriptions of multi-attribute nodes and edges into a common embedding space so their information can be aggregated. Second, the Heterogeneous Graph Decoupling framework includes an Anisotropy Feature Propagation module that learns effective propagation across multiple hops. This supports adaptive discovery of associations among attributes at large scale.

Benchmark results report a 28.93% accuracy improvement over existing methods. The authors also report downstream NDCG@20 improvement rates of 11.48% and 11.71%. These findings support UniHG as a resource for representation learning and cross-domain knowledge mining, together with a framework designed to address both semantic alignment and information propagation. The dataset and benchmark code are released.
neurips-2025-unihg-a-large-scale-univers.tldr: UniHG pairs a large multi-domain heterogeneous graph dataset with semantic alignment and adaptive propagation methods that improve benchmark and downstream performance.

paragraphs: Concept erasure modifies a diffusion model to stop it from generating a chosen concept. The paper asks how thoroughly such changes remove the concept from the model. It distinguishes two possible mechanisms: disrupting the model's internal guidance and lowering the concept's unconditional generation likelihood, potentially removing it entirely.

That distinction motivates several independent ways to probe an edited model. The authors supply visual context, alter the diffusion trajectory, apply classifier guidance, and inspect alternative generations produced in place of the targeted concept. Together, these probes examine the model through several routes that extend beyond attempts to recover a concept using adversarial text prompts.

The reported findings emphasize the value of this broader evaluation when assessing erasure robustness. A method's response to text inputs is only one aspect of the proposed assessment; visual information and changes to generation dynamics provide additional tests. The contribution is a conceptual framework for thinking about erasure mechanisms alongside a suite of probes for investigating whether suppression is robust across different interventions.
neurips-2025-when-are-concepts-erased-fr.tldr: The paper distinguishes possible concept-erasure mechanisms and introduces diverse probes to evaluate robustness beyond adversarial text prompts.
